title: When It Comes to the Personal Decisions of Team Members, Leaders Share Experience, Not Advice
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece distinguishes between giving advice and sharing experience when team members bring personal, non-work decisions to a trusted leader. The author argues that advice is prescriptive and carries the leader's authority, while sharing experience is descriptive and leaves the other person free to draw their own conclusions. Because personal decisions carry life-altering consequences, seasoned leaders resist the pull to tell people what to do and instead describe what happened to them or what they've observed. The piece frames this as a deliberate discipline rather than a dodge.
points: Being trusted enough to be asked about personal matters is a compliment, but also carries real risk if the leader's counsel is acted on.
Advice is prescriptive and closes a conversation; sharing experience is descriptive and opens one.
The line 'Here's what worked for me' versus 'Here's what you should do' captures the practical difference in language.
Seasoned leaders deliberately choose experience over advice specifically on personal, non-work decisions.
quotes: That’s why seasoned leaders never give advice regarding personal matters.
Instead of giving advice, they share their experience and allow people to draw their own conclusions and answers.
Advice carries authority and centers on the knowledge of the leader.
Experience carries humility and suggests the listener is the expert of their own life. Experience normally opens a conversation, where advice tends to close one.
Sharing experience says, “Here’s what worked for me,” whereas advice says, “Here’s what you should do.” Advice tells people what to think. Experience gives them something to think about.
